why.correct: Exports minus imports, goods and services together: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>300</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>120</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>380</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>90</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(300 + 120) - (380 + 90)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>420</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>470</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 420 - 470</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= -50</annotation></semantics></math>. Arland bought 50 billion arls more from abroad than it sold, a trade deficit.

The current account adds the balance of trade, net income and net transfers: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>45</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>30</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>−</mo><mn>25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-50 + (45 - 30) - 25</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= -60</annotation></semantics></math>. Purchases of foreign assets are not in it; they belong to the capital and financial account.

The two accounts sum to zero: current account + capital and financial account = 0, so the capital and financial account is <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>60</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">+</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-(-60) = +60</annotation></semantics></math>, a surplus. Arland paid for its extra purchases by selling 60 billion arls more of assets to foreigners than it bought from them.

The capital and financial account balance is foreign purchases of Arland assets minus Arland purchases of foreign assets: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>F</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>90</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">60 = F - 90</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>90</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>150</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F = 60 + 90 = 150</annotation></semantics></math> billion arls.
A foreign purchase of a Belvian asset brings money in: a credit in the capital and financial account.
options: Right: a foreigner is buying a Belvian asset, so money flows into Belvia and the purchase is a credit in the capital and financial account.
A bond is a financial asset, not a good or service. Asset purchases go in the capital and financial account.

options: An export of a good is a credit in the current account, not an asset trade.

options: A factory is an asset that will produce for years, not a good bought for use now; its purchase is a capital and financial account entry.

options: Right: Belvia pays for the extra transfers and imports by selling more assets to foreigners or borrowing more from them, so the capital and financial account balance rises by the same amount.

why.correct: The balance of payments is the record of all transactions between a country's residents and the rest of the world during a period.
options: That is the budget balance, a measure of government finances, not of transactions with other countries.

why.correct: Current account + capital and financial account = 0, so +35 is matched by -35.
options: The two balances sum to zero, so they have opposite signs: a current account surplus means a capital and financial account deficit.

why.correct: Income paid to foreigners (interest, dividends) is a current account debit.

why.correct: Turn the rate into arls per bel, <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>1.6</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0.625</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{1.6} = 0.625</annotation></semantics></math>, then multiply: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>300</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>0.625</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>187.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">300 \times 0.625 = 187.5</annotation></semantics></math> arls. why.correct: At 4 bels per arl, one bel costs <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0.25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{4} = 0.25</annotation></semantics></math> arl, so <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>800</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>0.25</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>200</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">800 \times 0.25 = 200</annotation></semantics></math> arls. why.correct: An appreciating arl makes arl-priced goods dearer for people paying in bels.

Government borrowing raises the demand for loanable funds, which raises the real interest rate.

why.correct: Expansionary monetary policy lowers interest rates, so the currency depreciates.

Right: net exports are a component of AD (C + I + G + X - M), and they fell by 70 billion arls, so AD shifts left.

why.correct: One country's net exports are the other's net imports.
options: Arland's imports are Belvia's exports, so when Arland's net exports fall, Belvia's rise.
The bel depreciated against the arl in the same move, which makes Belvian goods cheaper in Arland.
The bel depreciated, so Belvian goods became cheaper for Arland buyers.
Right: with two countries, Arland's exports are Belvia's imports and Arland's imports are Belvia's exports, so Belvia's net exports rose by 70 billion arls' worth.

why.correct: A depreciating currency makes the country's exports cheaper abroad.
options: Right: each arl now buys more bels, so coffee priced in bels is cheaper for Arland buyers, and they buy more.
The farms still get their bel price; what changes is that the coffee is cheaper for Arland buyers.
The bel price is the same, but the arl price is lower, and Arland buyers pay in arls.

why.correct: A depreciating currency makes imports dearer at home, so imports fall.
options: Each bel buys fewer arls, so arl-priced machines cost more bels, not fewer.

The arl price is the same, but Belvian factories pay in bels, and the bel price rose.

why.correct: Depreciation raises net exports, so AD shifts right.
options: A weaker bel raises exports and lowers imports, so net exports and AD rise.

Right: higher exports and lower imports raise net exports, a part of AD, so AD shifts right.
Net exports are spending, a part of AD.

why.correct: AD right in the short run: output up, unemployment down, price level up.
options: That would follow a fall in AD; here AD rises.
More output takes more workers, so unemployment falls in the short run.
Below full employment, a rise in AD raises output along the upward-sloping SRAS curve.
Right: AD shifts right along SRAS, so real output rises and firms hire more, lowering unemployment.

why.correct: An appreciation makes Arland exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper at home, so net exports fall and AD shifts left. In the short run the price level and real output both fall.

A depreciation makes Belvian exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home, so net exports rise and AD shifts right: the price level and real output rise in the short run. The axes are Real GDP and Price level.

why.correct: An appreciation hurts exporters: their goods cost more abroad.
options: Right: its wine now costs Belvian buyers more bels, so it sells less abroad.

why.correct: Lower net exports lower the current account balance; the capital and financial account balance rises by the same amount.
options: Right: net exports are part of the current account, which falls; the two accounts sum to zero, so the capital and financial account balance rises by the same amount.

why.correct: Financial capital flows toward the higher relative real interest rate.
options: Right: Arland assets now pay a higher real return than Belvian ones, so savers move funds into Arland, a capital inflow for Arland.
Savers move toward the higher real return, which is now in Arland.

The gap in real interest rates makes the net flow go toward Arland.

why.correct: The capital inflow raises demand for arls: the arl appreciates.
options: Foreign savers buying Arland assets need arls: they demand arls, they do not supply them.
More foreign savers want Arland assets, so demand for arls rises.
Right: to buy Arland assets, Belvian savers need arls, so demand for arls shifts right and the arl appreciates.
The funds come from abroad, so they must be changed into arls first.

why.correct: Higher real rate, capital inflow, demand for arls, appreciation, lower net exports.
options: The inflow is in the capital and financial account; through the stronger arl it lowers net exports.
The appreciation of the arl changes the prices that foreign and Arland buyers face, which changes trade.
An appreciation makes Arland exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper, so net exports fall.
Right: the stronger arl makes Arland goods cost more bels and Belvian goods fewer arls, so exports fall, imports rise and net exports fall.

why.correct: Lower real rates in Belvia send financial capital out of Belvia toward Arland.
options: Right: Arland assets now pay a higher real return than Belvian ones, so savers move funds toward Arland.
Belvia's real rates fell, so its assets pay less; savers move away from them.
A gap in real returns pulls funds one way: toward the higher rate.
Monetary policy changed the interest rates, and savers respond to the rates.

why.correct: Capital outflow: the capital and financial account balance falls and the current account balance rises.
options: Funds leaving Belvia to buy Arland assets are debits, so the balance falls.
Right: the outflow lowers the capital and financial account balance; since the two sum to zero, the current account balance rises by the same amount (the weaker bel raises net exports).
The two balances sum to zero, so they move in opposite directions.
The rates are not entries, but the asset purchases and trade they cause are.

why.correct: Lower relative real rates: more bels offered for arls, so the bel depreciates.

The currency moves with the demand for and supply of bels; here the supply of bels rises.

why.correct: In an open economy, expansionary monetary policy also works through a weaker currency and higher net exports.
options: Right: the weaker bel makes Belvian goods cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home, so net exports rise, adding to the rise in interest-sensitive spending.
